measures, they were not designed or powered enough to detect changes in vegetarian dish selection in the range of effects considered here. By contrast, Studies 8 and 9 are meant to test the effectiveness of the note on psychological measures, as well as serve as a rough indicator for vegetarian selection.

8\. Study 5: Assessing the Field Study Menu Intervention Materials

Study 5 aimed to assess two broad questions: First, what proportion of people would see and read dynamic norm messages in menus when considering what to order? Second, how do people interpret the information in the norm statement and its purpose in the menu?

8.1. Materials and Methods

8.1.1. Participants

Overall, 284 adults with a unique IP address in the United States took part, through Amazon’s Mechanical Turk in a “3–5 min Psychology Survey” for 45 cents.

This study was conducted at a time when an increase in “bot,” “click-farm,” and other suspicious activity had been observed on Amazon’s Mechanical Turk \[36\]. To address data quality concerns, we coded participants’ responses for potential evidence that participants were not from the U.S., using geolocation information and free response quality (see the Supplemental Material for full coding description); this method is similar to others that have been validated \[37\]. Coders achieved a high reliability (Kappa = 0.83). Discrepancies were resolved through consensus. Out of our total sample, 1.05% (3) responses were coded as likely coming from non-U.S. participants and were dropped from analysis.

Participants were shown the menu and asked to choose one item that they would like to order for lunch; if they chose more than one item, or specified a dish that did not resemble anything on the menu, they were dropped from analysis (2.14% of total participants). Additionally, participants were asked several free response questions; if they didn’t answer some of them, either by leaving a question blank or by typing something incoherent (e.g., “praba”), they were dropped from analysis (6.4% of total participants).

This left a sample of 257 participants. Of the remaining participants, 57.0% identified as men, 41.8% as women, and 1.2% as non-binary. The mean age was 35. The sample size was chosen to be sufficient to provide rough estimates of basic descriptive statistics about how many people would notice the note, and how they would interpret it. In Studies 5–9, all subjects gave their informed consent for inclusion before they participated in the study. These studies were approved by the Internal Review Board of Stanford University.

8.1.2. Procedure and Materials

Participants were told that we were doing research on food selection. They were asked to imagine they were buying lunch from a restaurant, told that they would be shown that restaurant’s menu, and would be asked to pick a single dish off the menu to order for lunch. They were randomly assigned to one of three menus, all from our field experiments. Menu A was from a campus restaurant that offers general American sports-bar fare, such as burgers, fries, and salads (Study 1). Menu B was from a high-end Italian restaurant (Study 3). Menu C was from a web-based restaurant branded as selling healthy meals, largely for lunch orders for businesses (Study 2). To adapt these menus to a national audience, some changes were made: ingredients and dish names on all of the menus were adjusted slightly to be more widely recognizable (e.g., switching from a “Pugliese Pizza” to a “BBQ Chicken Pizza”), and prices were adjusted to reflect more typical lunch pricing across the U.S. (lowered to $8–10 per entrée). Each menu had a variety of meat and vegetarian options. Vegetarian items were marked with a leaf, denoting them as “vegetarian” (Menu A), or containing “no meat” (Menu B), or each vegetarian item was directly labeled with the words “Vegan” and “Vegetarian” (Menu C). Using the materials from the interventions, each menu had a small note near the top with dynamic

Sustainability 2020, 12, 2453 20 of 38

norm information about a trend towards reducing meat consumption among restaurant customers (e.g., “We’ve noticed that our customers are starting to choose our meatless dishes for lunch more often”).

After indicating which dish they would order, participants were asked to recall what the note said (while the menu was no longer visible). Next, they were shown the menu again, and asked a series of questions.

8.1.3. Dependent Measures

Visibility and Recall

After the food ordering task, but before participants were shown the menu again, they were asked if they had seen, read, and could recall the note:

Did you notice the note, at the top right of the menu? (0 = No, 1 = Yes) Did you read the note at the top right of the menu? (0 = No, 1 = Partially, 2 = Yes) What were the contents of the note, that you remember? (Free response) Free responses were coded as either recalling the increasing popularity of vegetarian dishes (coded as dynamic norm), mis-remembering the note as about the static popularity of vegetarian dishes (static norm), simply as a promotion (no norm), copying and pasting text from the note or question (copied text), entering nothing (nothing), or other (Kappa = 0.85).

It is possible that asking participants whether they noticed or read the note could overestimate these occurrences, if participants feel obligated to report they saw the note, or underestimate these occurrences, if participants fail to recall that they had seen the note. By contrast, assessing their recall of the note’s content is a more conservative estimate of whether participants saw the note, as it requires them to reproduce it from memory. However, the latter indicates whether participants engaged with the note in a sufficiently attentive manner to recall it.

Interpretation of Note

While the menu and note were presented a second time, participants were asked four free response questions regarding how they interpreted the note. Each response was coded into exclusive categories developed through a reading of responses and noting common themes.

The first question was, “What do you think of when you read the note?”, which was coded as pertaining to one of eleven response types: commenting that the restaurant was accommodating its customers (coded as accommodating), speculating that the restaurant had good food (quality food), that the restaurant had vegetarian food (vegetarian food), that the food was healthy (healthy food), that the restaurant was trying to make money (money), that the restaurant wanted customers to eat vegetarian (prescribe vegetarianism), expressing support for the note (e.g., “It’s nice that they offer meatless options”, supportive), expressing opposition to the note (e.g., “I don’t care much for it”, unsupportive), identifying the reduction in meat consumption (dynamic norm), feeling that the note is pointless or trivial (trivial), thinking about people who are vegan or vegetarian (vegetarians) (Kappa = 0.88). Responses were also coded for the general valence as either positive, neutral, or negative (Kappa = 0.95).

The second question was, “Why do you think the restaurant put this note on the menu?” This question was coded for different rationales or motivations, including: to be inclusive of vegetarians (include vegetarians), to advertise products (advertising), to show customers that they are responsive to their wishes (responsive), to meet corporate social responsibility goals related to health or the environment (corporate social responsibility, or CSR), to save money or profit more (money), to encourage customers to consume less meat (prescribe vegetarian), and other (Kappa = 0.89).

The third question was, “What does this suggest to you about the restaurant’s food items?” This question was coded for different inferences about the dishes, including: that it was high quality (high quality), that the restaurant was accommodating or that the food selection was varied (accommodating), that the food was healthy (healthy), that the restaurant catered to vegetarians (for

Sustainability 2020, 12, 2453 21 of 38

vegetarians), that the meat products must be poor quality (bad meat), that some of the food has meat or vegetables (meat or vegetarian), that it didn’t indicate anything (nothing), and other (Kappa = 0.92). The fourth question was, “What does this suggest to you about the restaurant’s veggie dishes?” This question was coded for inferences about the vegetarian dishes, including: that participants thought the items must be new (new), that they must be high quality (high quality), that they were plentiful or available (plentiful), that they were poor quality (low quality), that they did not have meat (meatless), that they were popular (popular), that the restaurant wants customers to eat meatless (prescribe vegetarian), that it didn’t indicate anything (nothing), and other (Kappa = 0.93).

Note ratings. After the open-ended questions, participants were asked four questions related to the content in the note that we expected would impact how effective the note’s message would be, each using Likert responses:

How good or bad do you think their veggie items taste? (1 = Very bad, 7 = Very good) If you saw this at a restaurant, how believable or unbelievable would you find the note? (1 = Very unbelievable, 7 = Very believable)

How accurate or inaccurate would you think that this note is? (1 = Very inaccurate, 6 = Very accurate) How normal or strange do you think this is? (1 = Very strange, 7 = Very normal)

8.3. Discussion

There were several important findings from Study 5. First, few participants reported that they had noticed or read the notes used in our field experiments—only about one in three—and even fewer could recall the basic content of the note—less than 20%. Second, after being shown the note again, almost all participants had positive or neutral responses to it; few had a negative response. Yet, they have tended to interpret the note as about or written for vegetarians, such as to be inclusive to vegetarians, rather than thinking about the change in meat consumption as a broad trend pertaining to most people or people like them who ate meat. Thus, it appears the note could be improved in two major ways: first, by being more salient and thus noticed; and second, by appealing to all people, not assumed to be specifically for vegetarians or vegans, who are specifically not our target audience.

9\. Study 6: Assessing Psychological Reactance

Given that Study 4 found a backfire effect consistent with psychological reactance, Study 6 assessed whether notes encouraging people to eat less meat may lead people to feel coerced, including by comparison to a more traditional menu note, one that advertised specials.

The notes used in our field studies were designed to reduce reactance by including text that framed the dynamic norm information as emanating not from an effort to coerce patrons to eat less meat but as a response to customers’ preferences. To assess the effectiveness of this approach, Study 6 compares it to notes that contain a direct request to conform to the dynamic norm in the second line. Furthermore, this study examines how people interpret the intentions behind the restaurant’s choice to include the note on the menu. This includes more prosocial intentions (such as caring about health and the environment) or more coercive intentions (such as trying to get customers to buy a specific dish).

9.1. Materials and Methods

9.1.1. Participants

Overall, 479 adults with a unique IP address in the United States took part through Amazon’s Mechanical Turk in a “2–4 min Psychology Survey” for 40 cents. People who may have participated in Study 5 were ineligible. We used the same methods used in Study 5 to filter out potential non-U.S. respondents. Out of our total sample, 5.2% (25) responses were coded as likely coming from non-U.S. participants and were dropped from the analysis.

Participants were asked to choose one item that they would like to order for lunch; if they chose more than one item or specified a dish that didn’t resemble anything on the menu, then they were dropped from the analysis (0.4% of total participants).

This left a sample of 452 participants. Of the remaining participants, 41.6% self-identified as men, 58.2% as women, and 0.2% as non-binary. The mean age was 35. A minimum of 100 participants per condition, with four conditions, yields 80% power to detect medium-small effect sizes in differences between ratings of intervention materials (d = 0.4).

9.1.2. Procedure

As in Study 5, participants were told that we were studying food selection. Again, they were asked to imagine they were buying lunch from a restaurant and asked to pick a single dish from the menu to order (whether these choices were vegetarian are not analyzed for lack of statistical power). Unlike Study 5, Study 6 used a single menu, that from Study 3, the field study of lunch at a high-end Italian restaurant adapted for a national audience as in Study 5. The menu had a variety of meat and vegetarian options. This menu provided the template for Studies 6–9.

After indicating which dish they would order, participants were shown the note again, and asked a series of questions.

9.1.3. Manipulation

Participants were randomly assigned to one of four conditions in a 2 × 2 design. The note in each condition contained a dynamic norm, either about increases in orders for vegetarian dishes or for specials, depending on condition. Each note had a second line of text either with or without a direct request to order one of those items: “Try one of our \[Plant-based dishes/Specials\] today\!” Thus, participants were randomly assigned to one of these conditions: a vegetarian no request, a vegetarian direct request, a specials no request, or specials direct request (see Figure 5). Menus with notes about meat consumption marked vegetarian dishes with a leaf; menus with notes about specials marked specials with a star. The same items were marked for both specials and vegetarian items (i.e., all specials were vegetarian). The vegetarian no request condition uses the same note as Study 3, and is very similar to the notes in the over field experiments. very similar to the notes in the over field experiments.

Perceived Coercion

We assessed coercion with four measures. The first was a three-item scale with questions about how annoyed, pressured, or manipulated the note made participants feel (adapted from prior research \[34\]). Each was assessed using a Likert response:

“If you saw this while ordering food, to what extent would you feel annoyed?” (1 = Not at all annoyed, 5 = Extremely annoyed)

“If you saw this, to what extent would you feel that you were being pressured to order a \[meatless dish/special\]?” (1 = No pressure at all, 5 = A great deal of pressure)

“If you saw this, to what extent would you feel like people were trying to manipulate you?” (1 = Not at all manipulative, 5 = Extremely manipulative)

A second measure assessed how helpful or unhelpful participants found the note:

9.2.1. Perceived Coercion

In absolute terms, participants in the Vegetarian No Request condition—the note resembling our intervention in Studies 1–4—reported feeling between “not at all” and “a little” coerced on the 3-item scale due to the note, that is how annoyed, manipulated and pressured they felt. Despite this low mean, roughly 8% of participants felt either “moderately” or “a lot” of coercion. Importantly, these levels were significantly lower than among participants who saw the same note but with a direct request to order a vegetarian dish, suggesting the effectiveness of replacing the direct request with text emphasizing the responsiveness of the restaurant to customer preferences.

When the restaurant advertised specials, coercion was low regardless of the request condition, and did not significantly differ from the Vegetarian No Request condition.

Across conditions, participants did not feel the note was particularly helpful or unhelpful (M = 3.66, SD = 1.37). We found no differences on this measure by condition, F (2, 338) = 0.557, p = 0.573. (This comparison excludes the special direct request condition which was measured on a different scale.)

Participants felt no more annoyed by the prospect of a company generally advertising its vegetarian dishes than its specials: participants in the vegetarian note conditions anticipated feeling similarly annoyed (directionally less) than those in the special note conditions, t(448) = −1.63, p = 0.103. However, participants in both vegetarian conditions anticipated feeling “a little” annoyed if a company were to try to persuade them using the note to order a vegetarian dish. Further, they were more annoyed at the prospect of a restaurant using the note specifically to persuade them to order vegetarian dishes than specials, t (450) = 2.05, p = 0.041.

9.2.2. Intent

Nearly 70% participants in the Vegetarian No Request condition, which mirrored the note used in our field experiments, expected that the note was put there to attract vegetarians.

Participants in the Vegetarian No Request condition were more likely to think that the note they read was meant to improve the restaurant’s brand image, to show that the restaurant was being responsive to their customers, and was placed on the menu because the restaurant was trying to do something socially responsible for health or the environment, rather than trying to persuade them to buy certain dishes.

9.3. Discussion

In general, participants in all conditions reported feeling low levels of coercion (annoyance, pressure, or manipulation) due to the note, although 8% of participants who saw a note like the one used in our interventions felt at least moderate levels of coercion, which suggests there may be room for improvement. Further, the second line of this note designed to dissuade people from seeing the note as a direct request significantly reduced feelings of coercion. This note caused the same or less coercion than a similar note with an appeal to ordering specials.

Generally, the note used in the field experiments led to greater perceptions that the restaurant had prosocial intentions rather than coercive intentions. Regardless of the directness of the appeal, participants were much less likely to perceive the note to be persuading them to buy something when the note was about vegetarian items than when it was about specials, even when the vegetarian direct request appeal literally read, “Try one of our plant-based dishes today\!” When the note was about vegetarian items, participants were more likely to believe that the restaurant was doing something good, that the restaurant was responsive to customers wants, and that they were trying to improve their brand image. However, like Study 5, we find evidence that most participants thought the note was meant to appeal to vegetarians specifically, who are not our intervention’s target. Overall, this study provides evidence that the note is unlikely to harm perceptions of restaurants in any of the ways we examined, compared to traditional advertisements for specials in menus.

10\. Study 7: Increasing Visibility via Note Position and Medium

Study 5 found that people may not notice dynamic norm notes in menus. In a supplemental study, we tested one method of increasing visibility, simply making the note larger, which did not yield clear benefits (see Study S1). In Study 7 we attempt to increase visibility by moving the note to a more primary visual location, the top left corner of the page \[38\], and representing the text as a physical note appended to the menu. To help ensure that our attempts to increase visibility did not come at the cost of other important properties, we also include measures regarding the note’s perceived accuracy, if it is perceived as normal or as strange, and whether it causes people to feel coerced. If the note is perceived as inaccurate, strange or causes coercion, it may undermine the messages effectiveness.

10.1. Materials and Methods

10.1.1. Participants

1,025 adults with a unique IP address in the United States took part through Amazon’s Mechanical Turk in a “4–5 min Psychology Survey” for 50 cents. Those who may have participated in Studies 5–6 were ineligible to participate. The same criteria were used to drop participants as in Study 6, including 2.4% likely coming from non-U.S. participants, 2.2% of total participants for faulty dish selection, 7.9% for smart phone use, 9.6% for waiting for the page timeout, and 0.8% for failing to answer free responses.

This left a sample of 791 participants. Of the remaining participants, 47.7% self-identified as men, 52.0% as women, and 0.3% as non-binary. The mean age was 36.7. Roughly 200 participants per condition, with four conditions, yields over 80% power to detect medium-small effect sizes in differences between ratings of intervention materials (d = 0.3).

10.1.2. Procedure

Participants were given the same menu task and instructions as Study 6, followed by questions about the menu and note.

10.1.3. Manipulation

Participants were randomly assigned to one of four conditions: Control, Original Note, Corner Note, and Clipped Corner Note (see Figure 6). The control menu had no note. The remaining three conditions each had a note with the same text about a customer trend toward increasing selection of vegetarian items. In the Original Note condition, the note from Study 3 was used, and thus was on the right side of the menu, about one-third of the page down. The Corner Note condition approximately doubled the size of the note and font size, and put it in the upper left-most corner of the menu. Eye tracking research has found that the top-left corner is often viewed first when people scan a menu for something to purchase \[38\]. Further, the convention in English (and other languages) is that the top left is where one begins to read a document. The Clipped Corner Note condition was the same size and had the same placement as the Corner condition, but was printed on green paper and shown as if it were paper-clipped to the menu. This was meant to also take advantage of the custom of placing a physical note on top of another document to signal that it is meant to be seen first. Vegetarian items were marked with a leaf on both sides of the item name.

10.3. Discussion

Repositioning the note to the top left of the menu increased the visibility of the note, especially when it was paper clipped to the corner. However, many people still could not recall the contents accurately. We also found that participants felt less coerced by the Corner note than by the other two conditions. And placing a note in the corner was also seen as more normal and accurate than the original note.

While a paperclipped note may be hard to mass produce, an image of a colored note is highly scalable. In Study S2, we find that virtually the same benefits as the paper-clipped note can be achieved with a colored note on the menu (see Supplemental Material). Overall, it appears that a note with a contrasting color in the top left corner of the menu may enhance visibility: While the original notes used in the intervention were seen by roughly 25%–50% of participants in Studies 5–6, Studies 7 and S2 find that the Corner note and variants are seen by 60%–75% of participants.

11\. Study 8: Improving the Norm Referent

Studies 5 and 6 found that many people interpreted the note to be about or for vegetarians, rather than for people in general, let alone people who eat at least some meat—precisely the people who must be reached to reduce the consumption of meat. If meat-eaters think the message is not about people like them, it may be ineffective. How could the message be revised to increase the relevance of the social referent, so that customers see this message as being for and about people like themselves? One challenge in this setting is to find a referent that feels relevant to people in a generic restaurant context, where they may have little affiliation with their fellow customers (unlike members of a university community at a campus eatery, as in Study 1). Study 8 represents the dynamic norm in terms of a variety of referent groups that people may feel are relevant, including one that is directly about “non-vegetarians.”

Changing the norm referent might also impact important factors such as how believable the norm message is. For each condition, we assess the ratings of the note from prior studies (accuracy of the statement, whether it is strange or normal, if people find it sincere, and whether it leads them to feel coerced), as well as the proportion of vegetarian dishes ordered by each condition. Given that the effectiveness of the referent hinges on the note being read, Study 8 also uses the techniques from prior studies to increase the visibility of the note.

11.1. Materials and Methods

11.1.1. Participants

Overall, 1713 adults with unique IP addresses in the United States took part, through Amazon’s Mechanical Turk, in a “4–5 min Psychology Survey” for 50 cents. Those who may have participated in Study 5–7 were ineligible to participate. The same criteria were used to drop participants as in Study 7, including 4.1% responses likely coming from non-U.S. participants, 1.2% of total participants for faulty dish selection, 8.1% for smart phone use, 9.3% for waiting for the page timeout, and none for failing to answer free response questions.

This left a sample of 1324 participants. Of the remaining participants, 43.2% self-identified as men, 56.5% as women, and 0.2% as non-binary. The mean age was 36.9. Roughly 165 participants per condition, with eight conditions, yields over 80% power to detect medium-small effect sizes in differences between ratings of intervention materials (d = 0.35). Further, 7.2% of participants reported being vegetarian and were dropped from the analysis of whether their meal choice contained meat, leaving 1200 participants for that measure. In a comparison of the control condition against all note conditions, this study is 80% powered to detect an effect of a roughly 7 percentage point shift (e.g., from 18% to 25%). Notably, this would not be powered enough to detect the effects from our prior field experiment, but with improvements on visibility of the note now in place, larger effects may be possible.

11.1.3. Manipulation

Participants were randomly assigned to one of eight conditions: Control, Americans, Our Community, Customer Change, Customer Choice, Non-Vegetarians, People, and People Like Us. Further, two versions of the “customers” referent condition were created to help investigate the effect of emphasizing customers’ choice. Given prior findings on coercion, we felt it may be helpful to include language that reassured participants of their autonomy regarding food choice. In the Customers Change condition the subtext of the note read: “To accommodate this change, we offer great plant-based dishes,” while in the Customer Choice condition it read: “To accommodate this choice, we offer great plant-based dishes.” All other note conditions used the “change” language.

11.3. Discussion

Looking across the multiple indicators taken here, it appears that norm referents for “Community” and “Non-Vegetarians” are promising options for the intervention. These two conditions are the only ones to appear at the top or middle of the comparison set on measures of visibility, recall, sincerity, accuracy, normalcy, at the low end of coercion, and are trending higher in their proportion of vegetarian dishes selected.

12\. Study 9: Comparison to Original Note

Study 8 found that notes with dynamic norms that use “non-vegetarians” and “our community” members as referent groups lead to positive perceptions of the norm message and approached significance in ordering more vegetarian dishes. However, Study 8 was not well powered to detect smaller differences in vegetarian dish selection. In Study 9, we aim to compare these notes in a larger sample, with the improvements to visibility and referent groups, to the original note used in one of our field studies, as well as to a no note control.

12.3. Discussion

The Non-Vegetarian note outperformed the note originally used in Study 3 (and 4), in terms of vegetarian dishes selected and visibility. 13\. General Discussion

Across Studies 1–4, we incorporated dynamic-norm messaging into restaurant and the web-based menus in a scalable intervention to promote the consumption of vegetarian dishes. Studies 1–3 found modest increases in orders of vegetarian dishes from the intervention (1–2.5 percentage point shift of all purchases), although some these studies were underpowered and effects did not always reach significance. Further, exploratory analyses found substantial heterogeneity of effects in Studies 1–3. Study 1 found that the largest effects for patrons with a connection to the restaurant and the norm referent used, namely returning customers and members of the campus community at a campus eatery. Study 2 did not collect the full volume of observations planned, due to the abrupt closure of the business. With a smaller than planned sample, the intervention the 2.5 percentage point increase in vegetarian entrée orders observed was not significant. The originally planned study with the originally planned sample size did have sufficient power to detect an effect this size. Study 3 found a significant effect among the full sample, with lunch at a fine dining Italian restaurant. Meanwhile, in Study 4, which took place at the same restaurant as Study 3, but during the more expensive dinner hours, found the dynamic norm notes significantly reduced vegetarian ordering. Here, we also found moderation effects: customers who bought more items drove this backfiring effect, consistent with research showing that people who are higher in socio-economic status can experience reactance in response to social norms and thus resist such social influence to maintain their autonomy.

One interpretation for these results is that the dynamic-norm intervention may be better suited for contexts where people feel a connection with fellow customers (or other norm referents used), such as feeling they belonged to a common community, and less well suited for contexts where people are vulnerable to experiencing psychological reactance and thus resisting normative appeals, such as among wealthier customers at more expensive restaurants. However, the present studies were not designed to test these interpretations; thus, exploring them is an important direction for future research. Studies 5–9 identify a number of areas for improvement in the intervention delivery and contents. First, most consumers likely did not read the notes used in the field studies, due to poor visibility of the note. We find that the visibility of the note was improved by placing it in a visually prominent area of the menu (the top left corner) and by using contrasting colors. However, large numbers of participants still failed to accurately recall its contents. Second, a common interpretation of the note was that it was about vegetarians or catering to vegetarians; hence, meat-eaters would not believe the note was for people like them, and therefore were unlikely to be influenced by it. We found that the norm can be augmented by selecting a referent that meat-eaters have a connection to, whether a member of a common community (Study 1), or a group that clearly included them—“non-vegetarians” (Studies 8 and 9).

When these changes were implemented in online surveys, the note was more likely to be read, and potentially more persuasive in changing ordering than the notes used in Studies 1–4. However,

these results were on hypothetical lunch orders and were at times marginal or not significant in comparison to a neutral control. Moreover, critical comparisons of tests on ordering in online studies were underpowered to detect the small effects, 1–3 percentage point changes, that may be realistic in this context. Taken together, there appears to be substantial room for improvement in the development of a dynamic norm intervention in restaurant menus, which may yield stronger and more consistent results than those found in our initial field studies.

Effective, scalable, low-cost interventions to reduce meat consumption that have been rigorously tested under real-world conditions with large samples are not yet well documented. Considering that this intervention has little upfront or operational costs, even modest results may justify the inclusion of dynamic norm statements in restaurant menus.

Limitations and Future Directions

While the online studies in the present research begin to identify opportunities to enhance the impact of the intervention, field experiments with behavioral data remain the gold-standard for evaluating such improvements. We need field research to assess whether the changes documented here would produce more substantial and robust effects. Based on our results, future studies should assess notes that are (1) highly visible, (2) pretested to ensure customers have some connection to the norm referent used, so that the note is interpreted to be for and about people like them, (3) take place in settings that cater largely to working-class and middle-class customers, including fast food, fast casual, casual dining, premium casual, or family style restaurants, but not fine dining at dinner, and (4) be powered enough to detect effects as small as 1–3 percentage points.

Many psychological interventions find heterogeneity of effects across more representative samples \[25\]. While the exploratory findings demonstrating heterogeneity are substantiated by related research on social norms, confirmatory research would help clarify these effects, and thus identify where and with whom dynamic norm effects on meat consumption are stronger or weaker.

14\. Conclusions

We find that an intervention incorporating dynamic norms into restaurant menus to reduce meat consumption can yield positive but modest results, perhaps increasing vegetarian orders and reducing meat orders by approximately 2 percentage points across a number of real-world restaurant settings and online studies. Yet, this intervention can be improved in terms of its visibility and content, highlighting the possibility of larger effects. Generally, the costs of such an intervention are minimal, which may make even modest gains worth the investment.

title: How effective are messages and their characteristics in changing behavioural intentions to substitute plant-based foods for red meat? The mediating role of prior beliefs
authors: Annukka Vainio, Xavier Irz, Hanna Hartikainen
summary: The study used a population-based online survey experiment of Finnish adults (N=1,279) to test two message characteristics, message framing (health, climate, or combined) and refutation of misinformation, for persuading people to eat less red meat and more plant-based alternatives. It also tested whether prior beliefs about the health and climate impacts of red meat moderated these effects. Messages had a small but desired effect on intentions once prior beliefs were accounted for, and that effect was strongly moderated by prior beliefs. Messages changed intentions among 'meat-sceptics' but not among 'meat believers'. Combining frames and refuting misinformation was no more effective than single-framed, one-sided messages, so evidence that message wording determines effectiveness was limited.

1

How effective are messages and their characteristics in changing behavioural intentions to

substitute plant-based foods for red meat?

The mediating role of prior beliefs

Annukka Vainio

Xavier Irz

Hanna Hartikainen

Natural Resources Institute Finland (Luke), Helsinki, Finland

Address for correspondence:

Annukka Vainio

Natural Resources Institute Finland (Luke)

Latokartanonkaari 9

00790 Helsinki

Finland

E-mail: annukka.vainio@luke.fi

2

Abstract

By means of a population-based survey experiment, we analysed the effectiveness of two

message characteristics – message framing and the refutation of misinformation – in

persuading respondents to reduce their consumption of red meat and increase that of plant-

based alternatives. We also tested whether the effects of those two message characteristics

were moderated by prior beliefs about the health and climate impacts of red meat

consumption. The data were collected with an online survey of the adult population living in

Finland (N=1,279). We found that messages had a small but desired effect on intentions when

the effect of prior beliefs was taken into account, but that that effect was strongly moderated

by prior beliefs. In particular, messages changed behavioural intentions among the “meat-

sceptics” (i.e., those believing relatively strongly in the negative health and climate effects of

meat consumption) but not among the “meat believers” (defined symmetrically). The

combination of frames and refutation of misinformation were not found to be more effective

strategies than the provision of information through single-framed, one-sided messages. We

found limited evidence that the way a message is formulated determines its effectiveness in

changing behaviours.

Keywords:

framing; two-sided messages; beliefs; survey experiment; meat consumption; plant-based;

climate impact; health impact; meat substitutes

3

1\. Introduction 1

In high-income countries, the sustainability of current diets characterised by high 2

levels of processed foods, refined sugar, refined fats, oils and red meat is increasingly being 3

questioned due to strong adverse impacts on both the environment and human health (Tilman 4

& Clark, 2014). On the environmental side, food accounts for 15–30% of all greenhouse gas 5

(GHG) emissions (Esnouf et al., 2013), but there is evidence that this impact could be 6

reduced significantly through dietary changes involving a reduction in consumption of red 7

meat and substitution with plant-based alternatives, such as legumes and pulses. Thus, several 8

studies have demonstrated that nutritionally adequate vegetarian diets generate at least 20- 9

30% less GHG emissions than the average diet of a high-income country (Baroni et al., 2007, 10

Berners-Lee et al., 2012). On the health side, recent meta-analyses have documented a 11

probable link between consumption of different types of red meat and negative health 12

outcomes (Abete et al., 2014; Larsson & Orsini, 2014). In 2015, that evidence was deemed 13

sufficiently strong for the World Health Organisation (WHO) to classify the consumption of 14

red meat as probably carcinogenic to humans and the consumption of processed meat as 15

carcinogenic to humans (International Agency for Research on Cancer, 2015). Meanwhile, 16

there is now broad agreement and strong evidence that increasing intake of fruits and 17

vegetables protects against risks of various chronic diseases, including strokes (He et al., 18

2006), coronary heart disease (Dauchet et al., 2010), type-2 diabetes (Carter et al., 2010) and 19

some cancers (Pavia et al., 2006). 20

Reflecting this growing consensus about sustainable diets, dietary recommendations 21

in high-income countries now typically include clear advice to decrease consumption of red 22

meat and processed meat, and increase intake of plant-based products, especially fruits and 23

vegetables (e.g., Nordic Council of Ministers, 2014, p. 23). However, the academic and 24

policy literature remains sceptical about the ability of dietary recommendations and their 25

4

promotion by traditional informational measures, such as campaigns, to bring about 26

behavioural change (Irz et al., 2016). 27

A potential reason for this lack of effectiveness could be the confusion in the mind of 28

consumers about the health and climate effects of red meat consumption. In western food 29

cultures, many consumers believe that red meat is a healthy and even necessary part of a diet 30

(Verbeke et al., 2010; Wellesley et al., 2015). Moreover, most individuals living in Western 31

countries are still not aware of the negative impacts of red meat consumption on the climate 32

(de Boer et al., 2013, 2016; Lea & Worsley, 2003; Macdiarmid et al., 2016; Vanhonacker et 33

al., 2016) or are unsure about them (Pohjolainen et al., 2016). Disbelief in the climate impacts 34

of food was found to be the most important barrier to climate-friendly food choices among 35

young Finnish adults together with the perceived difficulty to change eating habits 36

(Mäkiniemi & Vainio, 2014) whereas belief that a behaviour mitigates climate change was 37

strongly related to intention to reduce meat consumption among the adults living in the U.S. 38

(Truelove & Parks, 2012). Consumers may also have both positive and negative beliefs about 39

red meat at the same time (de Boer et al., 2017). Understanding these beliefs is important 40

because individuals tend to evaluate new information considering how it fits with what they 41

already know (Thompson, 2013). 42

In order to identify ways to communicate to the public that red meat consumption is 43

both a health and a climate issue we need to understand the interplay between individuals’ 44

prior understandings and new information. Here two communication strategies are relevant. 45

The first strategy is framing and it operates by activating information that is already part of 46

individuals’ knowledge or belief structure (Nelson et al., 1997). Communicating the co- 47

benefits of behaviors by means of framing has become an important research topic in climate 48

change communication (Maibach et al., 2010; Myers et al., 2012; Petrovic et al., 2014). The 49

second strategy operates by means of helping individuals to relate their prior beliefs to new 50

5

information by presenting and refuting misinformation before presenting correct information 51

(Bedford, 2010; Lewandowsky et al., 2012; Osborne, 2010). Thus, in this study, we test these 52

two strategies: framing and refutation of misinformation, and different combinations of them, 53

paying particular attention to the mediating role of consumer’s prior beliefs. We follow the 54

definition of (Finnish) National Nutrition Council (2014) that defines red meat as the meat of 55

ruminants (beef or lamb), pork and processed meat products. The results will inform the 56

design of more effective ways of communicating dietary advice to get consumers to adopt 57

diets that are both healthy and climate-friendly. 58 59

1.1. Prior beliefs about red meat consumption and receptiveness to new information 60

With the term “beliefs” we refer to individuals’ prior knowledge (Chi, 2008) or 61

factual beliefs (Ahteensuu, 2012). Individuals’ beliefs usually support their food choices. For 62

example, individuals who consume red meat regularly tend to believe that eating red meat is 63

healthy, necessary, sustainable and ethical (Piazza et al., 2015). Frequent red meat eating has 64

been associated with positive beliefs about red meat (Berndsen & van der Pligt, 2004) and 65

climate change scepticism (de Boer et al., 2013). Individuals appear to have positive beliefs 66

about their own current diets and negative beliefs about diets that are different from their own 67

(Povey et al., 2001). 68

Individuals tend to avoid cognitive dissonance resulting from difference between 69

information, beliefs and behaviour (Cooper, 2007; Festinger, 1957), and, as a result, tend to 70

use multiple cognitive and behavioural strategies to maintain coherence between these. 71

Confirmatory bias, a tendency to trust in information that confirms one’s own prior beliefs 72

and behaviours is one cognitive strategy for maintaining coherence (White et al., 2003). For 73

example, highly health-conscious individuals have been found to avoid or reject information 74

that questions the healthiness of functional foods (Droms et al., 2009). Similarly, consumers 75

6

who believe that red meat is a necessary and healthy part of a diet have been found to avoid 76

or reject information that conflicts with their beliefs (de Boer et al., 2013). 77 78

1.2. Framing 79

In communication science (Chong & Druckman, 2007), a frame in communication 80

usually refers to the words, images, phrases, and presentation styles that someone uses for 81

presenting information (Gamson & Modigliani, 1989) whereas an individual frame refers to 82

an individual’s cognitive understanding of the issue (Goffman, 1974), such as meat eating (de 83

Boer & Aiking, 2017). In the context of food choices, framing in communication would mean 84

focusing on certain effects of food choices that are relevant to consumers’ understandings. 85

For example, most national dietary recommendations apply a health frame and do not 86

explicitly include environmental sustainability, and according to FAO (2016), there is a need 87

for integrated guidelines highlighting the links between health and sustainability. 88

Many individuals are more familiar with health issues and find them more personally 89

relevant than environmental issues, and therefore a public health focus is potentially a more 90

effective tool for strengthening climate mitigation support than the traditional environmental 91

focus (Nisbet, 2009; Myers et al., 2012). Perhaps for the same reason framing red meat 92

consumption as a climate issue has been found to be more challenging than framing it as a 93

health issue. For example, framing red meat consumption as a climate issue was ineffective 94

even among those Dutch consumers who were concerned by climate change (de Boer et al., 95

2016). Similarly, a German study found that reading newspaper articles focusing on animal 96

welfare or health effects of meat had stronger effects on intentions to reduce meat 97

consumption than the article focusing on the climate effects (Cordts et al., 2014). At the same 98

time, climate change concern has been found to be positively associated with self-reported 99

climate-friendly consumer choices among young Finnish adults (Mäkiniemi & Vainio, 2013; 100

7

Vainio & Mäkiniemi, 2016). Framing has also been found to affect attitudes about meat 101

consumption depending on individuals’ values (Graham & Abrahamse, 2017). Thus different 102

people may find different frames appealing, and it has been suggested that multiple frames 103

may lead to a wider acceptance than a single frame (de Boer et al., 2013). It has also been 104

suggested that the avoidance of certain words may be an effective strategy among some 105

groups, such as “climate change” among the climate sceptics (Moser & Dilling, 2011). 106

107

1.3 Refutation of misinformation 108

Messages that directly refute misinformation have been found to be another effective 109

persuasion strategy, which works by helping individuals to process conceptual 110

inconsistencies and facilitating the acceptance of correct information (Bedford, 2010; 111

Lewandowsky et al., 2012; Osborne, 2010). Messages that explicitly undermine 112

misinformation (refutational two-sided messages) have been found to be more effective than 113

simple messages or non-refutational two-sided messages (Allen, 1991; O’Keefe, 1999; 114

Wilson, 2007). For example, it appears that refutational techniques are more effective than 115

non-refutational ones in changing introductory psychology students’ misconceptions about 116

psychology (Kowalski & Taylor, 2009), and in changing individuals’ attitudes toward 117

economic sanctions against South Africa (Hale et al., 1991). However, there is also evidence 118

that the correction of beliefs is not always effective (de Boer et al., 2013; Kuklinski et al., 119

1998; Nyhan & Reifler, 2010). 120

121

1.4. Hypotheses 122

In the context of communicating to consumers about meat-based and plant-based 123

diets, we do not yet know which message characteristics are most effective and how these 124

message characteristics are moderated by consumers’ prior beliefs about food and eating. By 125

8

drawing on previous research, we wanted to test the effectiveness of two message 126

characteristics, message framing and refutation of misinformation, in persuading consumers 127

to change their future intentions to consume red meat and plant-based alternatives, taking into 128

account consumers’ prior beliefs about red meat. We developed four hypotheses focusing on 129

the effects of messages on intentions to make dietary changes and the role of prior beliefs. 130

We expected to find that reading a message (of any kind) would have a positive effect on 131

intentions (H1). We also expected to find that the effect of messages would be strongest in 132

the group that already had beliefs similar to the ones presented by the messages (Kuklinski et 133

al., 1998; Nyhan & Reifler, 2010) (H2). Moreover, we expected refutational messages to be 134

more persuasive than other messages (Allen, 1991; Hale et al., 1991; Kowalski & Taylor, 135

2009; O’Keefe, 1999; Wilson, 2007) (H3). The frame that combines health and environment 136

was expected to be more persuasive than the health frame or climate frame taken alone (de 137

Boer et al., 2013; Maibach et al., 2010) (H4). Moreover, in order to better understand the 138

characteristics of individuals with positive beliefs about red meat, we explored the 139

association between positive beliefs about red meat, gender, age, educational level and self- 140

reported consumption of red meat and plant-based products. 141

142

9

2\. Materials and Methods 143

2.1. Survey and experimental design 144

The data were collected through an online questionnaire using the consumer panel of 145

a commercial marketing research company, representative of the 18-65 years old internet 146

users living in Finland (N=1,279). The survey was distributed in August-November 2016. As 147

compared to the adult population of the same age range living in Finland, the participants 148

were more likely to be women and slightly older, have a higher level of education, and live in 149

the Helsinki-Uusimaa region (Table 1). About 15.7% reported following a plant-based diet, 150

10.9% were vegetarians and 2.3% vegans. There are no recent Finnish data with which to 151

compare those figures, but Vinnari et al. (2010) report that, in year 2006, 6% of Finns ate no 152

meat and 8% were defined as semi-vegetarian, with a clear positive time trend for both 153

proportions. 154

We used a population-based survey experiment approach with a between-subjects 155

design to test the effects of message characteristics on future intentions (Mutz, 2011). The 156

participants were randomly assigned either to the comparison group that did not read any 157

message, or one of the five test groups that read one of five different messages conveying 158

recommendations about food consumption. 159

160

167 2.2 Message design 168 Messages were developed using existing recommendations in Finland (Evira, 2017) 169 (see Appendix 1). The style of the messages was similar to the one that is typically used by 170 the public sector authorities when they provide nutrition and climate change mitigation 171

advice to the public. Visually the message was presented to the participants in the upper half

11

of the screen. 172

Messages included two main components. The first component of the message 173

included the experimental manipulation of message characteristics. The messages applying 174

climate frame mentioned the negative effects of red meat, and the positive effects of plant- 175

based alternatives on climate, and the messages applying health frame mentioned the 176

negative effects of red meat, and the positive effects of plant-based alternatives on health. 177

Refutational two-sided messages included the refutation of false beliefs about health or 178

climate effects of red meat before presenting the correct information. 179

The second part was the efficacy component and it was the same in all messages. It 180

explained how everyone could easily reduce the consumption of red meat and increase the 181

consumption of plant-based alternatives. The messages applying the health frame referred to 182

the recommendations by the (Finnish) National Nutrition Council (2014) and the messages 183

applying the climate frame referred to the recommendations by the Natural Resources 184

Institute Finland (2014); both are well-known Finnish public institutions providing 185

recommendations about food and eating. 186

Below the message the participants were requested to evaluate the message indicating 187

their agreement with the following statements on a 5-point scale (totally disagree – totally 188

agree): “The recommendation is convincing”; “The recommendation is clear”; and “It is easy 189

for me to apply the recommendation in my everyday life”. The purpose of these questions 190

was to make the participant stay on the message page for some time to reflect upon the 191

message, to control whether there were differences in persuasiveness and clarity between 192

messages and whether the participants perceived sufficient self-efficacy to follow the advice 193

(which was also the intended effect of the efficacy component). The comparisons of means of 194

different types of messages revealed no differences except that messages with a health frame 195

were rated as clearer (health messages M=3.850 vs. others M=3.724, p=.039) and easier to 196

12

apply in everyday life than other messages (health messages M=3.238 vs. others M=3.087, 197

p=.046). 198

199

2.3 Measurement of intentions, beliefs and past red meat consumption 200

After having communicated the messages, the participants’ intentions to change their 201

consumption of red meat and plant-based alternatives were measured with questions asking 202

how their consumption of six food items was going to change during the following 12 203

months. The food items were: the meat of ruminants (beef or lamb), pork, processed meat, 204

vegetables, legumes (a plant-based source of proteins often promoted as a meat substitute), 205

and plant-based dairy substitutes. There were six response categories: 1 (I don’t consume 206

now and will not consume in future), 2 (I intend to stop consumption), 3 (my consumption 207

will decrease), 4 (my consumption will not change), 5 (my consumption will increase), and 6 208

(I will start consuming). The responses were combined into two dichotomous variables. The 209

first variable was intentions to reduce or discontinue consumption of red meat products 210

(original response categories 2 and 3) and the reference group were those who did not intend 211

to reduce or discontinue (original response categories 1, and 4–6). The second variable was 212

intentions to start or increase consumption of plant-based products (original response 213

categories 5–6), and the reference group were those who did not intend to start or increase 214

(original response categories 1–4). About 40.90 % per cent of the respondents (N=523) 215

intended to reduce or discontinue their consumption of red meat and about 31.20 % per cent 216

of the respondents (N=399) intended to start or increase their consumption of plant-based 217

2.3. Methods 247

We used binary logistic regressions to test hypotheses H1 to H4 and linear regression to 248

explore the association between beliefs, participants’ socio-demographic characteristics and 249

past red meat consumption. The participants having been randomly assigned to groups, socio- 250

demographic variables were not included in the models as control variables when testing the 251

hypothesized effects (see Mutz, 2011). The logistic regressions were specified in two 252

different but equivalent ways in order to assess both the total effect of each message on 253

intentions and the specific contribution of each message characteristic to that total effect. In 254

all cases, interaction terms between the variables measuring beliefs and messages or message 255

characteristics were introduced to assess the possibility of prior beliefs influencing the effect 256

of information provision on intentions to change behaviour. The coefficient estimates are 257

reported with their p-values and, unless otherwise specified, the default level of statistical 258

significance is 5%. 259

4\. Discussion and conclusion 347

4.1. The findings and their interpretation 348

This study examined the influence of prior beliefs about red meat -based diets on 349

consumers’ response to persuasive messages encouraging them to adopt a plant-based diet. 350

By means of a population-based survey experiment, we compared the effectiveness of 351

different message characteristics, including framing and refutation of false beliefs, as well as 352

combinations of characteristics, in shaping behavioural intentions. 353

In line with expectations, we found that reading any message was positively 354

associated with intentions to change behaviours when the effect of prior beliefs about red 355

meat-based diets was taken into account. At least in this narrow experimental setting, we 356

therefore conclude that information had the desired effect on behavioural intentions, but also 357

that individuals’ prior beliefs played a key role in determining responses to persuasive 358

20

messages. Beliefs moderated the effect of reading a message on behavioural intentions as 359

expected: reading any message changed behavioural intentions among “meat-sceptics” but 360

not among “meat believers”. Beliefs were also found to influence intentions to change 361

behaviours directly: beliefs that red meat -based diets were healthy, climate-friendly and 362

necessary were negatively associated with intentions to increase consumption of plant-based 363

products. These findings are in line with the confirmation bias literature suggesting that 364

people are more easily persuaded by information that confirms their prior beliefs about an 365

issue (de Boer et al., 2013; Droms et al., 2009; Lewandowsky et al., 2012; Thompson, 2013; 366

White et al., 2003). 367

The results about message characteristics did not entirely conform to expectations 368

and, in particular, we did not find evidence that refutational strategies were more effective 369

than non-refutational strategies at modifying consumers’ behavioural intentions. This finding 370

contrasts with those of previous studies that have established the superiority of refutational 371

strategies in changing behavioural intentions (Bedford, 2010; Lewandowsky et al., 2012; 372

Osborne, 2010). 373

Our study also found limited support that the way a message is framed matters. In the 374

context of persuading consumers to adopt plant-based diets the use of multiple frames has 375

been suggested as an effective strategy (e.g., de Boer et al., 2013). Against expectations, we 376

did not find any evidence that applying a combination of health and climate frames was more 377

effective than the single-frame messages in modifying intentions. This finding also differs 378

from that of a German study where the climate frame was found to be less effective than the 379

health frame in forming future intentions to reduce meat consumption (Cordts et al., 2014). 380

Part of the explanation for these differences could be technical, as we controlled for 381

respondents’ red meat -related beliefs which were found to be strongly associated with 382

behavioural intentions. 383

21

Older participants, males, and those with a relatively low level of education were 384

more likely to endorse positive beliefs about red meat -based diets. These beliefs were also 385

strongly associated with a frequent consumption of red meat and infrequent consumption of 386

plant-based products. These findings are entirely in line with previous research suggesting 387

that individuals tend to maintain a coherence between beliefs, past food choices and future 388

intentions (Berndsen & van der Pligt, 2004; de Boer et al., 2013; Piazza et al., 2015; Povey et 389

al., 2001). 390

Limitations. Inevitably, our study presents a number of limitations that should be kept 391

in mind when interpreting the results and drawing conclusions. We only measured the effect 392

of messages on intentions rather than actual behaviours, which is an important limitation 393

given the evidence of a frequent intention-behaviour gap in relation to food consumption 394

(Tang & Bhamra, 2009). However, changes in intentions being a necessary condition for 395

behavioural change, our results nonetheless generate valuable insights - for instance 396

regarding the lack of responsiveness of those with favourable prior beliefs about red meat 397

consumption to persuasive messages promoting the adoption of plant-based diets. Another 398

limitation is that we did not measure the effect of messages on beliefs, which may themselves 399

change as respondents acquire new knowledge about the health and climate effects of food 400

consumption. At another level, we analysed respondents’ self-reports of their beliefs, 401

intentions, and past behaviours, which are subject to social desirability bias (Chung & 402

Monroe, 2003). It seems that there were slightly more vegetarians and vegans in the sample 403

than it is estimated to be in the Finnish population (Vinnari et al., 2010), so there may be 404

more meat sceptics in the sample than in the Finnish population. A surprising finding of our 405

study is that the specific message characteristics under investigation had only a limited 406

impact on behavioural intentions. It may be caused by other message characteristics that were 407

present in all messages, thus potentially confounding the impact of framing and refutation of 408

22

misinformation. For example, the messages mentioned the (Finnish) National Nutrition 409

Council and the Natural Resources Institute Finland as information sources. Although those 410

are two well-known public institutions in Finland, the credibility of each source may have 411

also affected the persuasiveness of the messages, as source credibility has been shown to 412

matter in other contexts (e.g., Pornpitakpan, 2004). It is also possible that the respondents 413

were already familiar with the contents of messages of the study, which might have reduced 414

the impact of these messages. Finally, we grouped health and climate related beliefs together 415

and did not study their effects separately. It is possible that some red meat -related beliefs are 416

more important than others in hindering or facilitating the acceptance of messages about 417

plant-based diets, which is an issue that should be explored further in the future. 418

419

4.2. Conclusion 420

Despite these limitations, we suggest that these results increase our understanding of 421

why it is so challenging to change food habits by means of information provision, and what 422

kinds of strategies may be effective in changing behaviours. Consumers who are regular red 423

meat eaters and infrequent consumers of vegetables are often those who also have strong 424

positive beliefs about meat eating. In this group, communication through messages is not 425

likely to be an effective strategy because people tend to avoid situations where they have to 426

face a cognitive dissonance. However, messages were effective in modifying behavioural 427

intentions within the group of meat-sceptics, probably by confirming beliefs that were 428

already held. It is also possible that repeated exposure to messages may reveal long-term 429

changes that were not measured in this study but should be explored in the future. It appears 430

that ambivalent attitudes and beliefs are more likely to be changeable than those that are not 431

ambivalent (Povey et al., 2001); for example, ambivalent meat eaters are more likely to report 432

intentions to reduce their meat consumption in the future than those who are not ambivalent 433

23

(Berndsen & van der Pligt, 2004). Thus, it is possible that exposure to messages increases 434

ambivalence in respondents’ beliefs, which is not directly or immediately seen in intentions. 435

Overall, the findings highlight the importance of understanding individuals’ prior 436

beliefs about food and eating in order to devise effective means of encouraging them to adopt 437

plant-based diets. However, more research is needed to understand the process by which 438

individuals make sense of message contents. Targeted communication based on a careful 439

understanding of target groups’ prior beliefs is needed. In the current era of social media and 440

“post-truth”, it has become increasingly important to help individuals gain scientific literacy, 441

for example through debiasing campaigns (Lewandowsky et al., 2012). Consumers need help 442

to learn to select and read information critically so that they will be able to assess and 443

distinguish between information that is valid and not valid. We therefore suggest that the 444

developers of information campaigns do not simply aim at filling the “information deficit” 445

but rather identify novel strategies helping consumers to make sense and process 446

contradictions and uncertainties in information about healthy and climate-friendly diets in an 447

effective way as part of their daily lives. 448

title: Making plant-rich dishes work: Practical solutions from food service operators
